openalex_display_name: Dirt in Victorian Literature and Culture: Writing Materiality
openalex_abstract: Sabine Schülting presents scholars with an original approach to the impact of dirt, waste, and unwanted material items on nineteenth-century British fictions, colonial narratives, social treatise, and Victorian Britain's physical and cultural landscapes. Schülting plants her research in the ripe field of material culture studies, building upon the work of Elaine Freedgood, Andrew H. Miller, Mieke Bal, Arjun Appadurai, and Peter Burke. She reminds us of the complicated nature of the very term “dirt,” ultimately defining it as “Matter [which] disturbs order and threatens to pollute what a social group cherishes as clean and pure” in her undertaking “to look for those shock moments when dirt arrests the flow of language and ‘asserts’ itself as matter” (6–9). She traces such instances through fictions by Victorian authors Charles Dickens, Elizabeth Gaskell, and George Gissing (briefly touching on George Eliot and George Henry Lewes), as well as early modernists George Moore and Henry James, but Schülting reaches beyond the confines of literature as she stretches her examination of dirt into social essays, travelogues, biographical excerpts, and even nineteenth-century print advertisements. These textual investigations support her thesis that these writings reveal to modern readers the ways dirt affected individual lives, cities, and even British colonies; additionally, she posits that these writings shaped their contemporary public's response to abundant waste and even cultural attitudes toward materiality. In short, Schülting's new work illuminates dirt's impact on nineteenth-century writings, and how these writings shaped the way nineteenth-century Britons confronted, conceptualized, and dealt with dirt.In her first chapter, “Dirt and Victorian Thing Culture,” the author explores the Victorian obsession with amassing material goods, maintaining cleanliness, and the concept of recycling—namely, strategies for repurposing items and ideas for repurposing waste. Touching upon stereotypical figures such as the miserly Jewish peddler and the deceitful Irish trader, Schülting explains how conceptions of bustling trade on the poverty-ridden streets of London contrasted with the celebrated materiality of the Crystal Palace and emerging department stores in a multitude of ways: “open—closed, dark—bright, old—new, chaotic—ordered … clean-fraudulent, honest—the other” (20). Her claims are rooted in Henry Mayhew's London Labour and the London Poor, which argues that for the lower classes of London, “wealth [was] not the result of manufacturing new commodities, but rather, of recycling old things and waste matter” (21). Applying these insights to Victorian literature, particularly Our Mutual Friend and Bleak House, Schülting explains how the “curiosity shops and heaps of dust and refuse” in Dickens's novels “are not just alternatives to Victorian commodity culture, but examples of … the narrative potential of old things and waste matter” (36). The most discerning analysis in this chapter explores the manner in which the recycled clothing in Our Mutual Friend reflects the personalities of their fictional wearers.In the following chapter, “Dirt, Disease, and Death,” Schülting presents us with Mayhew's disturbing descriptions of the slime, squalor, and filth that contaminated the streets and infected the lives of those living in London's slums. Weaving in Edwin Chadwick's Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain, she reveals the shocking nineteenth-century misconception that such an accumulation of dirt was reflective of lower-class complacency, which supposedly “allowed” such poisonous sludge to amass (54). She notes that upper-class society viewed cholera as a plague the struggling classes brought upon themselves. By linking Punch cartoons focused on cholera epidemics and “The Great Stink” of 1858 to Dickens's Great Expectations and Gaskell's Mary Barton, Schülting ties the social prejudices fostered by these epidemics to the injustices experienced by characters such as Joe the blacksmith and Jem. Applying this connection to other Victorian fictions, she argues that George Eliot attributed Daniel Deronda's Mordecai's terminal illness to his impoverished living conditions in order to shake stereotypical judgments about the “dirty lower classes.” She argues that Victorian authors like Eliot killed off their sympathetic characters with the more “romanticized illness” of tuberculous to rejuvenate public compassion for those who suffered in the dirt because they had no alternative (55).For those primarily interested in Victorian fiction, chapter 3, “Slum Biographies,” contains Schülting's most intriguing and insightful analysis. She opens with Dickens's essay “A Nightly Scene in London” in which he describes five impoverished women sitting outside a workhouse as “great beehives, covered with rags,” barely discernable as people (79). Schülting is particularly interested with the way Dickens's lengthy, sympathetic description of one of these women strips her of her identity as a sexual, gendered being, effectively revealing how “dirt and emaciation have transformed the woman's body to such an extent that … it only references death” (81). Schülting finds similar instances in Dickens's Sketches by Boz, Our Mutual Friend, and Bleak House, as well later works, including George Gissing's The Unclassed and Arthur Morrison's Child of Jago, as she demonstrates how such wrenching narratives of poverty “move from the margins to the center of fictional literature about urban slums, thus challenging the concept of the autonomous subject and … the Bildungsroman as the dominant form of narrating selfhood” (81). Focusing on Krook's death by spontaneous combustion in Bleak House, she refers to George Henry Lewes's letter published in The Leader, in which he described the episode as “a fault in art and fault in literature … giving currency to a vulgar error” (93). In opposition of Lewes, Schülting finds merit in the incident by considering its implications within the context of associating humans with trash and waste. She points out that the German chemist Liebig (whom Lewes cites in his letter) “stressed that a substance that was brought into contact with putrefying matter would itself be affected by putrefaction,” meaning the clean and pure would be corrupted by the dirty and impure (93). By reading Krook's death as being caused the putrefying items in his warehouse, Schülting redefines his demise as a commentary on the impact of the gross materiality of poverty on human lives.Her final chapters, “Urban Emotions” and “Rewriting Indian Dirt,” present concise investigations into the anxiety and disgust that displaced upper-class empathy for the poor residing in London's slums, and the ways colonizers used narratives of dirt to defend their assumed superiority, in turn inspiring postcolonial writers to later challenge these condemnations. In “Urban Emotions,” the author acknowledges that the nineteenth-century realist novel's goal was to provoke sympathy and tackle social inequities, but also claims that in these fictions, “disgust turns out to be embedded in the circulation of affects.” And while she sees reductive binaries of good and evil, clean and dirty, innocent and guilty in works like Oliver Twist, she champions Gaskell's Mary Barton for evoking a “complex vision of the healing of social problems through sympathetic identification with those who live in revolting dirt of poverty” (119). The richest part of this chapter explores Henry James's often overlooked Princess Casamassima, which she reads as a mockery of upper-class notions of detached sympathy for lower-class characters by forcing the book's gentleman protagonist, Hyacinth, into direct contact with the miserable reality of the slums.In “Rewriting Indian Dirt,” Schülting presents us with nineteenth-century print advertisements for Congo Soap and Pear Soap, each depicting exotic locales within the colonies, therefore synonymizing “imperial expansion with the international spreading of British ideals of hygiene” (160). She connects this documented xenophobic fear of contamination to E. M. Forster's A Passage to India, which offers critical, detailed, condemnatory descriptions of Indian excrement, mud, dilapidation, social lethargy, and superfluous rubbish. The heart of the chapter identifies Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi (written in 1940, set in 1911) as a direct response, and challenge, to Forester's reductive and condemnatory narrative of “Indian dirt” (168). While Schulting compares Twilight in Delhi to the “poetics of disintegration characteristic of late-Victorian fiction,” her chapter seems detached from the rest of the book, the topics of dirt and British literature insufficient anchors to tie it back to the work's title.Victorian scholars will benefit from the wealth of critical approaches to and variety of textual accounts of dirt Schülting offers her readers. Dirt in Victorian Literature and Culture benefits from the depth of Schülting's research and her well-earned expertise on the topic. Yet, as she delves into established theoretical approaches to literature and materiality, or historical trends in investigating the grimier aspects of the nineteenth-century landscape, her own voice seems to dim beneath the weight of the information provided. Her close readings of Dickens, Gaskell, and Gissing incite the question: Why is George Eliot so overlooked? Close considerations of works like Felix Holt and Daniel Deronda would have further illuminated Schülting's revelations about the impact of dirt on nineteenth-century society. Finally, the book would have benefited from a conclusion, one bearing more of Schülting's own insightful analysis, which shines in the book's introduction and its most insightful chapter, “Slum Biographies.”SUSAN RAY is an assistant professor of english at Delaware County College where she teaches composition and British literature. While her research primarily focuses on Victorian Studies, it also includes American dime novels and pop culture studies. Her recent publications include “The Imprint of the Western Dime Novel on Hard-boiled Pulp Fiction” in Gale Cengage's critical anthology Hard-boiled Fiction and “Thackeray: Poking Holes in the Narrative of Empire” in Victorians: A Journal of Literature and Culture. She is currently researching the impact of William Thackeray's traumatic childhood on his psyche, and in turn, his fictions.

openalex_display_name: P akistani Fiction
openalex_abstract: There has always been a tradition of English‐language writing in Pakistan, but contemporary Pakistani English fiction is new. In 1947, when Pakistan was created by the partition of British India, its only eminent English‐language novelist was Ahmed Ali. His classic Twilight in Delhi (1940) portrays life in traditional Delhi against the onslaught of Westernization and provides interesting contrasts with Sunlight on a Broken Column (1963), a requiem for Lucknow by the Indian writer, Attia Hosain. Ali's innovative, stylized linguistic experiments foreshadow the more successful strategies of Hosain and Pakistanis Aamer Hussein and Kamila Shamsie to incorporate the literary elements of Urdu into English narrative.

openalex_display_name: Realism in the Twentieth-Century Indian Novel: Colonial Difference and Literary Form
openalex_abstract: Ulka Anjaria's Realism in the Twentieth-Century Indian Novel challenges conventional ways of understanding both realism as a form and the formal attributes of Indian fiction. Over five chapters, it details the emergence and development of the realist novel in India from the late nineteenth to the middle of the twentieth century. It offers a thought-provoking reexamination of key novels in Hindi, English, and Bengali, including Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's Anandamath, Rabindranath Tagore's Ghare Baire, Munshi Premchand's Godan, Mulk Raj Anand's Coolie, Raja Rao's Kanthapura, Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi, and Bibhutibhushan Bandopadhyay's Aparajito. Anjaria argues that whereas magical realism has come to be privileged both as the hallmark of third world and postcolonial writing, and as the method that such writing uses to challenge the politics of colonial modernity, in colonial and newly independent India realism was the mode through which writers engaged with questions of colonial injustice, nationalism, the hierarchies of class and caste, and the urban–rural divide. Realist narratives allowed them to debate what form modernity should take in India, and conversely, such debates enabled their wide-ranging experiments with realism. Thus, Anjaria argues, the aesthetic innovations and political visions of Indian realism enabled one another. In the hands of the novelists she discusses, realism was a heterogeneous practice that defies some of the distinctions critics have made between it and other modes of representation.Anjaria opens her book by remarking that whereas studies of European and American novel have recognized that realism is not simply a “naïve, mimetic representation of an inert and legible world, postcolonial criticism continues to regard the term with embarrassment” (4). Her aim, she declares, is to show that “realism in the colony” was in fact shaped by a self-consciousness on the part of novelists about their difference from Europe and its forms of realism, and “an awareness” of their “secondary status within colonial discourse.” It was this awareness and distance, in part, that allowed Indian writers to play with genre, and to bend realism to accommodate their own concerns. But such remolding was also the result of their own attempts to engage with questions of equality and freedom in India. Thus, Anjaria rightly insists, “realism is a mode of engagement, innovation and imagination within writing under colonialism, rather than … [a] colonial leftover” (29). But Anjaria's work achieves more than a revaluation of simply Indian realism. Her discussions illuminate the limitations of any theoretical understanding of realism that derives only from a reading of European and American fiction. Instead of then seeing Indian novelists as only reshaping established Western norms of realist writing, we might better understand their work as demonstrating that realism, understood as a global practice, is a far more capacious and varied mode than is commonly understood.However, the force of this argument is compromised by Anjaria's insistence that all these novelists were engaging in a self-conscious dialogue with European realism and its derivations in India. Such insistence results in an explicit privileging of the novelists' aesthetic agendas over their political concerns, which runs counter to her declared agenda as well as to what I see as the real implications of her study. Thus, for example, in chapter 2, Anjaria offers a persuasive reexamination of Munshi Premchand's famous novel Godan, which is widely recognized as realistically detailing the harsh reality of rural poverty. Anjaria demonstrates that Godan in fact acknowledges how much of this harsh reality cannot be depicted. Premchand suggests that what is necessarily excluded by his representation is also ignored by Indian nationalism, and even by left-wing visions of India. In this way, Anjaria argues, Premchand both advances and questions the promise of Indian nationalism as well as the capacity of realism. However, as this fine argument is advanced, she conflates established modes of (European) realism, humanism, and mainstream Indian nationalism. So, for example, early in the chapter, Anjaria quotes Elizabeth Ermarth as suggesting that “the genial consensus of realistic narration” reinforces “the uniformity at the base of human experience and solidarity of human nature.” From this, she concludes that realism necessarily implies a commitment to “humanist uplift” and an understanding of humanity as an organic whole. Thus, she writes, “Premchand suggests that realism on its own will not bring about human equality but rather must balance its utopic vision for common humanity with a simultaneous awareness of the reality of difference” (45). But surely it was nationalism rather than realism that was the object of Premchand's critique. Surely, too, despite the commitment of some realist writers to a utopic vision, much realist fiction has been historically committed to exploring difference (of class, of gender, of religion, and in India, of caste and colonialism). It is one thing to argue that Premchand's experiments with form are inextricable from his social and political visions, and quite another to suggest that any literary writer or program actually assumed that realism “on its own” would bring about social change.A similar privileging of formal experimentation and, consequently, a flattening of realism is also evident elsewhere. In an otherwise fine chapter on Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi, Anjaria suggests that realism necessarily works with a model of “linear, progressive time” (107), one that is particularly conducive to being appropriated by bourgeois nationalist ideologies as they suggest the utopic development of an “imagined community.” Ali self-consciously complicates such an appropriation by his depiction of nostalgia among the Muslim elite, and suggests that such nostalgia indicates their alienation from the dominant narrative of Indian nationalism. But inasmuch as nostalgia is not simply an object of Ali's analysis but also becomes his own mode of representation, and inasmuch as his novel demonstrates that “the nation” was never a singular space in India, surely in the first place Twilight in Delhi alerts us against a reductive equation of realism with linearity, and of the nation with “empty homogenous time.” Indeed, Anjaria seems to suggest as much when she writes that it is “postcolonial theory beginning with Benedict Anderson” that has misunderstood the multiple temporalities in which a nation always exists (108). If it is a certain theory of the nation and the novel that has gotten it wrong, rather than “realism,” then should we not understand Indian realisms as emerging from a different history of the nation? In India, nationalisms emerged unevenly across diverse regions and among different religious and cultural and linguistic communities, so that the relationship between nationalism and “the novel” (and indeed nationalism and print culture) as posited by Anderson in his Imagined Communities must necessarily be qualified. This is the case even when—or especially when—novels strain to discuss the possibilities of a pan-Indian nationalism (as is the case with Indulekha, O. Chandu Menon's 1889 Malayalam novel). Despite the fact that a hegemonic pan-Indian nationalism did emerge, these competing visions did not simply dissolve, but rather animated and complicated literary imaginations in every part of the country. Of course, this is not to suggest that there were no shared features between novels in different languages, or that Indian novelists did not ever self-consciously argue with Western literary theories and practices, or those who sought to transplant them to India. Given the engagement of the Progressive Writers in India (a group that includes most of the writers Anjaria discusses) with European socialism, that would be a ridiculous assumption. Indeed, one of Anjaria's achievements in this book is to contest the critical view that the formal innovations of the Progressive Writers happened in spite of, rather than because of, their political visions.The need to rethink the relationship between literary realism and nationalism is most sharply demonstrated through Anjaria's examination of novels written between 1925 and 1940, each of which features Gandhi as a character. Even though I cannot agree that in these novels Gandhi is presented largely as “a crucible of literary experiment” (97), Anjaria offers a fine-tuned examination of how both Mulk Raj Anand's Untouchable and Raja Rao's Kanthapura use Gandhi to probe the limits of Indian nationalism, and reflect on the relation of individuals to the nation by reanimating allegory as a method. They demonstrate that allegory is not antithetical to realism (as is generally presumed) but an intersecting mode of signification. In her final and perhaps most compelling chapter, Anjaria shows how Satyajit Ray's films Aparajito and Apur Sansar remake, in the idiom of “modernist realism,” an earlier novel by Bibhutibhushan Bandopadhyay which is marked by a Romanticist desire to create characters and a narrative style that will transcend the details of everyday existence. Anjaria is most persuasive when she demonstrates how realist fiction is formally because politically supple, and how formalist experimentation accompanied (rather than impelled) debates about progressive nationalism. The longing for, and the fractures of, realist form are thus part of the challenges faced by Indians who desired not just freedom from colonialism, but also freedom from other oppressive hierarchies. While gender is startlingly absent as a concern in Anjaria's account of this body of fiction, and one cannot help wishing she had dealt with at least one woman writing in India, the major achievement of this book is provoke us to rethink the global lineages and the formal as well as political attributes of realism.

openalex_display_name: A li, A hmed
openalex_abstract: Ahmed Ali was an Indian fiction writer, poet, and translator who wrote in both Urdu and English. He published his first novel, Twilight in Delhi (1940), in the same decade as the founding trinity of Indian fiction in English, R. K. Narayan, Mulk Raj Anand, and Raja Rao published theirs, but his career did not unfold to match theirs. His two other slim novels, Ocean of Night (1964) and Of Rats and Diplomats (1985), have long been out of print; neither came close, in any case, to the inspired vision and artistry for which Twilight in Delhi is acclaimed as a minor classic.

openalex_display_name: Bilingualism in Pakistani Fiction: The Analysis of Twilight in Delhi by Ahmed Ali
openalex_abstract: This research aims to find code-switching occurrences in Twilight in Delhi written by Pakistani English postcolonial writer Ahmed Ali. He uses many Urdu terms and expressions in his narrative to keep alive Eastern culture and traditions that would otherwise lose their essence if translated into English. In this way, he reconstitutes English language in his work. The frequency of Urdu words is recorded, and the data obtained is analyzed on semantic, phonological and syntactic grounds. The writer also tries to experiment with the form and brings creativity, and in doing so, he applies English structure on Urdu terms and introduced a new vocabulary. The deliberate use of code-switching in the novel shows that language is no one’s property neither someone’s hegemony. Keywords: Bilingualism, Code-switching, Pakistani English, Post-colonialism

openalex_display_name: Representation of Implicit Domestic Culture in Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi
openalex_abstract: Exploring implicit domestic culture in Twilight in Delhi (2007)by Ahmed Ali, the study applies theoretical framework of M.A.K Halliday’s Systemic Functional Grammar (SFG) which asserts that meanings lies in the clause. The main argument of the paper is to linguistically examine the effects of social imbalance within family structure. It also argues that language is not neutral for it carries ideology in it; therefore, hegemonic power relations and its manipulation are explored leading to its effects on different lives.Data are analyzed qualitatively at clause level, using tools of ideational, interpersonal and textual meta-functions of language.As a guide, 19 Tables are formed to show and compares the processes according to the main issue of the study. Linguistic analysis of the text is done by using Transitivity, Mood, Rheme and Theme to identify power relations in Eastern families. The paper examined different sorts of 19 situations where the norms of implicit family culture were noticed. The study also discovered that the male members of the family exercised power over the female characters. The study is going to be an addition to future researchers of CDA to use SFG to literature to highlight and analyze social imbalance.

openalex_display_name: Study of Socio-Cultural Transition in Twilight in Delhi with reference to Vygotsky’s Sociocultural Theory
openalex_abstract: The study investigated Socio-cultural aspects in novel 'Twilight in Delhi' by Ahmed Ali published in 1940.It analyzed the cultural and social transition that the sub-continent was going through during the British rule in the region.Vygotsky's sociocultural theory has provided the theoretical framework for the study which describes how the society plays its role in learning and shapes the behavior of the individuals.Qualitative research has been used and the content analysis of the primary data has been made which has been taken from the text of the novel.The findings indicated how the behavior of the main characters was transformed as they come under the influence of two different cultures.It was identified that younger generation mainly represented through the character of Asghar was more influenced by the British culture than his elders like Mir Nihal primarily because both grew up in different socio-cultural settings.

openalex_display_name: Comparative Analysis of Twilight in Delhi and A Passage to India through the Lens of Stylistics and Postcolonialism
openalex_abstract: While focusing on the postcolonial discourse, a comparative analysis of A Passage to India(1924) and Twilight in Delhi (1940) has been carried out.The former writing was composed by western author E.M. Forster while the latter was written by South Asian author Ahmed Ali. In both writings, the center of focus is the effects left by colonizers on colonized land,specifically in terms of culture, norms, and values. In order to complete the study in a profound manner, a qualitative approach has been employed in which description, analysis, narrative devices and definitions are utilized as research tools to affirm the deductive approach of the study. The paper is analyzed through postcolonial perspectives with a focus on discourse and stylistics viewpoints of the texts. Political, cultural,communal, social, and religious conditions of the subcontinent are unfolded from the standpoints of informant and colonizers with the implication of dichotomous critique while looking at the miserable situation of the Asian colonized region. As one author belongs to the class of colonizers and the other has its roots in colonized land, the study has explored various similar as well as contrasting elements from the novels.

openalex_display_name: Pandemic as a Disaster
openalex_abstract: Does pandemic literature come under the domain of disaster studies? How have realist modes of writing become effective and fitting to focus on social issues and posit themselves against orthodoxy, fundamentalism and aloof nationalist literary practices? How can we read the narratives of suffering and “risk” in a text when the world has moved towards “second modernity”? This chapter attempts to engage with these few questions, however, not limited to them, through the reading of Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi from a neo-historical as well as from an eco-critical perspective. The 1918 influenza flu or Bombay Fever which provides a definite backdrop for this novel also opens up the possibility to discuss the effacement of this pandemic from the Nationalist historical discourse of this country. Twilight in Delhi is a trend-setting novel of the progressive and realist mode of literary practice in India. Founded with the publication of Angarey in 1932, this literary movement achieved its political radicalism and revolutionary voice with more maturity in the novel. Touching upon many issues of the time ranging from nationalism, progressive writing, protest against orthodoxy and fundamentalism, love, marriage, pining, death and the influenza flu, the novel records a time and lifestyle of a community on the verge of a massive change and challenges and also a new writing style capable enough to acknowledge it.

openalex_display_name: Manifestation of Colonial Subjects in Twilight in Dehli and A Passage to India
openalex_abstract: The goal of this research is to examine how the colony is portrayed by both the colonizer and the colonized. This paper focuses mainly on the politics of depiction by implementing the insights of postcolonialism. In this context, Twilight in Delhi by Ahmed Ali also deals with the same subject from the view of the colonized, whereas A Passage to India is a narrative of the British colony by its colonizer E. M. Forster. It may be argued that the writers’ two depictions of a similar colony represent different political and cultural viewpoints. The two authors’ representations of the same colony, one from a colonized civilization and another from that was colonized, consistently reflect their distinctive voices. Additionally, the latest research has incorporated Homi K. Bhabha and Edward Said’s analytical works on the depiction in the postcolonial theoretical perspective and explored the problem of cultural representation while using textual analyses. The research has shown that both works’ representations of colonial India differ significantly because of the authors’ respective cultural roles as colonizer and colonized.

openalex_display_name: The Politics of Representation of the Colony A Critical Study of A Passage to India and Twilight in Delhi
openalex_abstract: The current study aims to investigate the colony and its representation by the colonizer and the colonized. By applying the theoretical insights of postcolonialism, this paper will focus on the politics of representation. In regard to this, A Passage to India is a record of the British colony by the colonizer E. M. Forster, whereas, Twilight in Delhi by Ahmed Ali too deals with the same but from the perspective of the colonized. Arguably, the authors present the same colony in two different ways which exhibit their cultural and political positions. The representation of the same colony by the two authors one from the colonizing civilization and the other from the colonized is always reflective of their individual voices. For Edward W. Said, the West represents the East in a way that helps in presenting a dominating a position of the West and it represents the East as inferior, superstitious, uncivilized and evil. Moreover, the current study has probed the issue of cultural representation by employing textual analyses and applied Homi K. Bhabha and Edward Said’s theoretical works on representation in postcolonial theoretic paradigm. The analyses have shown that both the texts represent colonial India quite differently because of the cultural positions of the writers as the colonizer and the colonized.

openalex_display_name: 14 UNHOMING THE PIGEON: AHMED ALI’S TWILIGHT IN DELHI
THROUGH THE OPTIC OF EDWARD SAID'S ORIENTALISM, UNMASKING IDENTITY; EXAMINING THE IDEAS OF "SELF" AND "OTHER" IN AHMED ALI'S TWILIGHT IN DELHI
openalex_abstract: My heart aches to see you fight for chairs; Only poor masses are crushed with open arms by bears. I saw many deaths in houses and houses in deaths, But thou made me unable to breathe. We are drowning up to the neck in our blood; No one is there to come, see and judge masses smeared with mud Never ever tell the truth to live a life, Dumb, deaf, and blind can live here. (Farman Ullah) Informed by the close reading of the novel Twilight in Delhi (1940) by Ahmed Ali during and under the impact of colonization from the perspectives of sociopolitical aspects of the extraordinary situation that has been faced by common people through ordinary words. The present study aims to examine the novel Twilight in Delhi, how the "“Self”" and the "“Other”" interact within the historical backdrop of British colonialism and the "massacre and destruction in Delhi in 1857" (Yahya: 2013) as it is portrayed in the book Twilight in Delhi. It contends that prejudice, an imbalance of power, and oppression characterize this relationship. The research looks at the negative effects of this uneven dynamic, such as violence, theft, and cultural fusion. The novel's author gives the colonized Indians a voice by denouncing British colonial power and urging resistance to it. The conclusion emphasizes the necessity to confront and end colonial dominance while highlighting the harmful impacts of the "“Self”" and "“Other”" connection.

openalex_display_name: Exploring Double Colonization in Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi and Buchi Emecheta’s The Joys of Motherhood: A Comparative Analysis
openalex_abstract: The present study puts its emphasis on the cross-cultural study of double colonization in Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi and Buchi Emecheta’s the Joys of Motherhood. Double colonization refers to a situation where women face oppression by both patriarchy and colonialism. The experiences of such doubly colonized women appear bitterer than their Western counterparts as they are always being subjugated on the basis of race, culture and gender. A feminist postcolonial perspective of Twilight in Delhi and The Joys of Motherhood, from Gayatri Chakravarty Spivak’s point of view, aims to reveal manifestations of double colonization of Indian and African women in the novels and the oppression these female characters face both as women and as the colonized. Textual analysis of the novels Twilight in Delhi and The Joys of Motherhood further gives the impression that this double colonization of the female characters has shattered the family relationships as the women appear to lose their attraction on account of different psychological problems resulting from their double oppression. Moreover, there appear many points of convergence and divergence during this cross-cultural study of double colonization of Indian and African women.

openalex_display_name: Unhoming the Pigeon: Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi
openalex_abstract: Pigeons’ storied history and waning fortunes have drawn the attention of many writers, including Ahmed Ali. Ali’s 1940 novel Twilight in Delhi uses pigeon imagery to link together the spatial trope of homelessness and the temporal trope of slouching toward extinction. The novel is about the long decline of a Muslim family under British imperial rule. Its patriarch often meditates on the tragedy of cultural extinction, and his pigeon loft is made a synecdoche for that threatened culture. Early critics frequently read Twilight as a nostalgic lament for the Mughal Empire that preceded British occupation in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. However, as more recent scholarship has argued, Ali likely intended for his novel to be, not a call to restore the lost precolonial past, but a way of using residual elements of that past to galvanize a postcolonial future. This chapter argues that Twilight in Delhi, like other twentieth-century texts, makes pigeons emblems of homelessness and extinction, but it also refigures the birds as a sign for survival, futurity, and change. In Ali’s vision, those who are in the wrong place or the wrong era are also those who point to other possibilities for social and political life, beyond the cultural and biological depredations of British occupation. This was a powerful anticolonial message in the 1940s. It can be powerful again today, in the era of climate change and the sixth extinction, as an insistent call to make the victims of imperial capitalism—including displaced people and displaced animals—the center of the just community that, one hopes, will succeed us.

openalex_display_name: Pandemic India: From Cholera to Covid-19
openalex_abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic was/is a curious time for historians of medicine and public health. A moment when our work became immediately and uncomfortably relevant to an especially wide audience as people looked to the past to make sense of the present. In this richly sourced book, David Arnold decolonizes these pandemic histories and centers India as pandemic source and site, as laboratory and observational space.Arnold begins by situating his book against the broader scholarship, but he also explores what a pandemic means and settles on four broad “pandemic propositions”: that pandemics are recurring historical phenomena; that pandemics have spatial and temporal presence; that pandemics are exceptional events; and last, that they are both subjective and epidemiological phenomena. His first case study is, appropriately enough, cholera, the “first modern pandemic” (38). Cholera's emergence as a pandemic in the nineteenth century is undeniably intertwined with the histories of the British Empire in particular, but this chapter situates cholera specifically within Indian ecologies of water and connects the pandemic to labor, religion, and the colonial economy. One of the most striking conclusions of the chapter is the devastating toll of cholera for Indians in general (for example, the region accounted for as much as 80 percent of global death tolls from cholera between 1817 and 1920 [68]). Cholera also holds the distinction of being the catalyst for modern thinking about pandemics and sanitary reform across the world, as well as truly unprecedented international cooperation and coordination from the mid-nineteenth century onward in particular.The book's exploration of plague in India echoes many of the themes that emerged in the cholera chapter, underscoring how pandemics disproportionately impacted the already vulnerable and marginalized. India was among the worst affected regions during the third plague pandemic, but it disproportionately impacted Dalits, the poor, and those struggling with scarcity and famine. Plague also precipitated tensions between the Indians and the British, which culminated in riots. This chapter also describes how colonial anxieties around the plague culminated in one of the draconian public health legislations in British India, the Epidemic Diseases Act of 1897, which was subsequently invoked during COVID-19.In the chapters on influenza, Arnold is unequivocal about the toll of this disease: “Influenza was the greatest epidemic disaster India ever experienced, at least within the annals of recorded history.” Like the plague, the bustling commercial port of Bombay served as a locus for the disease, and Arnold traces how troop mobilizations in India in the First World War escalated transmission and contributed to dramatically higher death rates from influenza for sepoys relative to British soldiers. The case of influenza also reiterates exactly how the Indian experience of pandemics was exacerbated by poverty, scarcity, and famine. Beyond the metanarrative of influenza, Arnold also captures everyday life during a pandemic, but it is perhaps the fifth chapter that shines the most for me. This chapter painstakingly traces the intentional and unintentional acts, at all levels, that contributed to the eventual and remarkable “forgetting” of the millions who died and those left behind to live with those losses. Arnold describes the political, structural, and rhetorical techniques that the colonial state deployed to erase the pandemic. Immediately after the 1918 pandemic, India saw a wave of memorialization of those sepoys who had fought in the Great War and the nearly one million Indians who had died. However, pandemic influenza and the dead emerge only occasionally and uneasily in literature, newspapers, and other narratives from the time, except for Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi (226). The chapter ends with a sober reminder of the contemporary dangers of these acts of erasure and forgetting.In the next chapter, though, Arnold notes that if the “Spanish Flu” was a “forgotten pandemic” in India, then AIDS was even more the “absent horseman of the Indian apocalypse” (242). Colonial neglect and apathy might have exacerbated the toll of prior pandemics, but with AIDS and COVID, Arnold delineates how the multiple failures and compounding omissions of independent India have resulted in a state uniquely ill prepared for pandemic crisis by any global standard. The book also includes an exceptional account of the progress of the COVID lockdown and the deployment of the plague-era Epidemic Diseases Act to re-create conditions that reminded many Indians of the infamous emergency. The lockdown abandoned and stranded the most vulnerable—the laboring poor. The chapter also rightly notes how social media and press coverage produced an extensive visual archive of this historical moment. Most Indians and observers remember those striking photographs of stranded and devastated migrant laborers, of burning funeral pyres, of people struggling to breathe, of people dying in hospital parking lots—a visual counterpoint to the state's own narratives of the pandemic.Pandemic India reminds us that India has always been and continues to be central to the global histories of pandemics, yet it does not lose sight of the essential interconnectedness between India and the rest of the world that shaped the experiences and flows of pandemic diseases. But Pandemic India is not a narrative that examines pandemics as a transnational epidemiological phenomenon alone; this book is anchored by Indians’ own perceptions and quotidian experiences of pandemics. The book ends with a deliberation of what history offers in moments of pandemic crisis, the possibilities of considering the reflections and refractions of this moment in the past. What do we gain and lose when we look at the past solely with the intent to understand the present pandemic moment?

openalex_display_name: Languishing in Ahmed Ali’s Delhi
openalex_abstract: Ahmed Ali, a founding member of the All-India Progressive Writers Association (PWA), was castigated for his first novel in English which failed, according to its critics, to address the pressing needs of India’s poor and suffering. Ali’s Twilight in Delhi is surprisingly committed to passivity, given the writer’s pioneering affiliation with the activist group. Instead of representing activist struggle, his novel depicts the death of a culture and its lingering afterlife, ironically via the English language and literary form. While there is no doubting the novel’s opposition to empire, it embraces passivity as a formal challenge to the ideological demands of the PWA, whose members openly derided it. Two fragile cultural forms linger even after their extinction in the novel: Urdu poetry, especially the ghazal form, and the ancient art of pigeon-keeping. In the end, the novel aligns itself with the vanquished and vulnerable – whether art or animal – and submits to an imperial form that will paradoxically ensure their survival.

openalex_display_name: Last embodiments of Traditionalism: Comparing Responses to Colonialism in the Protagonists of "Twilight in Delhi" and "Things Fall Apart"
openalex_abstract: This comparative analysis examines how the protagonists in Ahmed Ali's "Twilight in Delhi" and Chinua Achebe's "Things Fall Apart" respond to colonialism's cultural and political influence on their societies. This study examines how the protagonists, Mir Nihal and Okonkwo, symbolize traditional values and beliefs threatened by colonial forces, drawing on postcolonial literary theory. This analysis reveals how the protagonists' responses to colonialism differ, with Mir Nihal striving to protect traditional values in the face of colonial encroachment. However, Okonkwo's response is characterized by violent resistance. This paper also examines how colonialism affects cultural identity and traditionalism in India and Nigeria, including social structure and language changes. Finally, this study contends that the characters' responses to colonialism in these novels can be used to comprehend colonialism's more significant cultural and political effects on traditional civilizations.

openalex_display_name: COMPARING INDIAN AND WESTERN RESPONSES TO PANDEMICS: EXISTENTIAL CRISES IN REBATI, A LIFE MISSPENT, AND TWILIGHT IN DELHI
openalex_abstract: This paper explores the existential themes in Indian and Western pandemic narratives, focusing on how pandemics are depicted in literature and their impact on human experience. Through a comparative analysis of works such as Rebati by Fakir Mohan Senapati, A Life Misspent by Suryakant Tripathi Nirala, and Twilight in Delhi by Ahmed Ali, alongside Western texts like The Plague by Albert Camus, The Last Man by Mary Shelley, and Love in the Time of Cholera by Gabriel García Márquez, this study examines how pandemics serve as catalysts for existential crises and reflections on mortality, love, and human connection. In Indian narratives, pandemics often highlight social decay, personal suffering, and the impact of colonialism, while Western narratives engage more directly with existentialism, absurdism, and resistance. In García Márquez's novel, love becomes an existential response to death, providing meaning amidst suffering. By contrasting these narratives, this paper demonstrates that while pandemics bring death and despair, they also offer profound reflections on life’s meaning. The study shows how different cultural contexts shape literary responses to disease, illustrating both shared human concerns and distinctive cultural interpretations of suffering, mortality, and the quest for meaning. Ultimately, this comparative study offers new insights into the role of pandemics in shaping existential thought.

openalex_display_name: A Review of Literary Representations of Pandemics, Epidemics and Pestilence
openalex_abstract: During the COVID-19 lockdown, a group of writers from an online magazine community, Café Dissensus, came forward to develop on the growing readership virally directed towards a niche genre of outbreak narratives. The first online issue released in 2021 under the editorship of Nishi Pulugurtha was sooner improvised and made available in print format in 2023 as Literary Representations of Pandemics, Epidemics and Pestilence. The collection is dedicated to interest “the students of English literature, social science, gender studies, cultural studies, psychology, society, politics and philosophy” (Pulugurtha 2021, Editorial note) and general readers, given its broad mapping of contagious environs. The volume of sixteen chapters is open and creative in its interpretation of pan/epidemics through the lens of literature, films, letters, and even digital obituaries.This book has a timely release as a crucial improvisation of Pandemics and Epidemics in Cultural Representation (Venkatesan et al. 2022)—focusing exclusively on how contagious cultures were historically negotiated till the present. The chapters are divided into the following sections: 1. Memory and Contagion; 2. Uncanny Dilemmas; 3. Moving between Language and Media; 4. Fear, Disaster and Dystopia; and 5. COVID-19, Public Health and Social Justice. Instead of bringing a fluid transition between the chapters, this arbitrary division and ordering of the chapters makes the collection seem more broken. A much better scale for the grouping and aligning of chapters could have been devised based on the genre, timeline, or geography or demography in context.The review picks all the chapters based on the suggested layers of classification to delve in-depth into the sociocultural intricacies it speaks of. Dealing with Indian literatures from the colonial era, Subham Dutta’s chapter narrates on the “Epidemic Anxiety and Narrative Aesthetics in Sarat Chandra’s Palli Samaj and Pandit Mashay,” which exhaustively deals with epidemics as “co-texts” in Bengali literature (2023, 72). The chapter stands out with its formalist development in making efforts to self-translate Bengali passages to English. It delivers a crucial problem addressed by unveiling how many vernacular texts focusing on pan/epidemics are untranslated and inaccessible to the larger public readership. Sipra Mukherjee and Ishan Mehandru, in this collection, conduct a comparative reading of Suryakant Tripathi Nirala’s Kulli Bhaat with two different short fictions, Fakir Mohan Senapati’s Rebati and Rajinder Bedi’s Quarantine, respectively. Sipra Mukherjee requests “a different literary approach” (18) and “different way of thinking” (23) when it comes to comprehending epidemics via Indian vernacular literature—however, fails to offer conclusive findings on different methodologies. Ishan Mehandru vocally declines Agamben in the Indian context by addressing how “the plague does not germinate a state of exception” given India’s history of consisting of a priori “exceptional people” who only become explicitly vulnerable during pan/epidemics. In chapter 12, Sumantra Baral focuses on a single text, Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi, from the lens of Robert Paine’s no-risk thesis to critique the political milieu of colonial India, which remained in denial towards the 1918 Spanish Flu as it gripped colonial Delhi. Subarna Bhattacharya’s chapter purloins a letter written by Pandita Ramabhai, “a firebrand women’s rights activist” (128), to The Bombay Guardian in 1897. Via the letter, she explains the covert sexual abuse suffered by Indian women during the Bombay Plague, stating a historic “urgency to save brown women from white men and white women” (136) rephrasing cultural critic Gayatri Spivak. In Indian literature, the repetitive reading of the same text, like Nirala’s Kulli Bhaat in certain chapters, further indicates a dearth in the availability and accessibility of exhaustive and extensive Indian literature surrounding outbreaks.The collection compensates for such a vernacular gap with its coverage of world literature and texts from other media. However, repetition is inevitably found here, as well, with Daniel Defoe’s A Journal of The Plague Year being dealt with in comparative (transgeneric and transmedial) reading by Amit Baishya and Sanghita Sanyal. While Baishya offers a minimalist reading of the opening sequences of the latest Hollywood film World War Z and Defoe’s Journal, Sanyal compares Defoe’s entry with its pop-culture manifestation, The Periwig Maker, a stop-motion puppet animation film. Sacaria Joseph, following a similar format, continues his philosophical deliberation on Albert Camus’ The Plague by shuffling between biblical references to locate the “absent God” (84) during times of disaster-like outbreak. Sarottama Majumdar and Tania Chakravertty cleverly unveil the semi-biographical undertone of Mary Shelley’s The Last Man and Katherine Anne Porter’s A Pale Horse, Pale Rider, offering scope for life-writing outbreak experiences within creative spaces. Riti Agarwala “deal(s) with the gap” (57) of the porous, thin line between fiction and nonfiction in The Decameron, where storytelling during a crisis renders a cathartic experience. Goutam Karmakar’s chapter on Pandemic and Man-Less Society is a hypothetical assessment of Sweeney-Baird’s The End of Men. The idea of how “only men carry the virus [and] only women can save us” (44) is highly metaphorical towards patriarchy where the chapter critically locates “trans women and gay men” as super-minority vis-à-vis doubly marginalized. (Post)modern fiction’s popularization of the outbreak as foreseeing dystopic futures is elucidated by Paramita Dutta’s exploration of Jack London’s The Scarlet Plague and Sayan Aich Bhowmik’s reading on Margaret Atwood’s Oryx and Crake focusing its relevance on contemporary warfare politics. Following a discussion on a similar thread, Tabish Khair brings out a Marxist analysis of “quasi-vampire” and “quasi-zombie” adaptations to offer a neo-populist model to attend informal migrant workers who are treated as “superfluous” (172) living-dead in the neoliberal necropolis. The final chapter by Yash Gupta stands out in its thoroughly critical yet creative analysis of digital obituaries as literary texts vis-à-vis the birth site of posthumous identities.This collection primarily exhausts mainstream pan/epidemic narratives as a contribution towards global crisis literature—noting it as a responsible act of cultural materialism exhibited for nurturing pandemic preparedness. It leaves further room for discussion in terms of including a larger array of narratives, both oral and written, particularly from vernacular cultures and languages, to strongly reflect on Indigenous perceptions of pandemics, epidemics, and pestilence.

openalex_display_name: IMPERIAL NARRATIVES AND NATIVE VOICES: A COMPARATIVE POSTCOLONIAL STUDY OF TWILIGHT IN DELHI AND HEART OF DARKNESS
openalex_abstract: The literature addressing colonialism have been produced both by colonizers and colonized. The variances of their perspective on colonialism can be found in their writings. This study, using textual analysis, explores Heart of Darkness by Joseph Conrad and Twilight in Delhi by Ahmed Ali through the lens of postcolonial theory, focusing on the psychological, cultural, and political ramifications of colonialism. The study is qualitative in nature, and the sample passages for analysis from the novels have been selected by using the technique of purposive sampling. Conrad’s work critiques the moral corruption and inhumanity embedded in European imperialism, using Africa as a symbolic landscape to reflect the inner darkness of the colonizers. In contrast, Ali’s novel presents an intimate portrayal of cultural decline and identity loss under British colonial rule in India. While Heart of Darkness reveals the dehumanizing effects of colonial power from the oppressor’s perspective, Twilight in Delhi captures the emotional and cultural disintegration experienced by the colonized. Together, these texts illuminate the complex dynamics of power, resistance, and historical memory central to postcolonial discourse. The significance of the study lies in the fact that it can be used by the teachers, researchers and students as it develops the understanding about the analysis of text written on the subject of colonization.

openalex_display_name: A New Historicist Analysis of Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi
openalex_abstract: The aim of this paper is to shed light on the novel Twilight in Delhi by Ahmed Ali through the lens of New Historicism which highlights the connection between the literature and the historical period of the work creation. Holding the background of early twentieth-century Delhi, the novel portrays the social and political turn of the Mughal empire and the British rule. The method used for this research paper is qualitative method with descriptive approach. This paper seeks to determine how the text portrays a decaying Delhi through comparing the narrative representation of the social relations and contexts with the documented histories and cultural text from the period of British colonialism and the resulting social crises for a society as depicted by Ali. The analysis of the novel and new historicist approach leads to the key argument, suggesting that Ali points at a postcolonial disintegration of the city and its decaying culture as a metaphor for the breakdown of the civilization under colonial rule. Consequently, this paper affirms that Twilight in Delhi is not only a literary piece, but also a historical account that opens a window into the cultural and political climate of the period. Hopefully the findings of this research will help the future researchers to study the novel from the historical, social and political context.

openalex_display_name: Ahmed Ali's twilight in Delhi : selected essays
The Reconfiguration of Core and Periphery in Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi and Aravind Adiga's The White Tiger
openalex_abstract: This essay discusses Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi published in 1940 and Aravind Adiga’s The White Tiger published in 2008 as two distinct examples of writers from the subcontinent employing specific stylistic devices to respond to particular periods of historical crisis through their fiction. This essay looks at the use of setting, language, intertextuality and other stylistic modes that the narratives adopt to address the historical and socio-cultural crisis that they grapple with at two distinct junctures in the city’s and by implication India’s history.In this paper I argue that both authors pick and choose literary and stylistic devices to create an amalgamation of techniques that can meaningfully represent the specific historical crises their works deal with. To contextualize my methodological praxis it is necessary to refer to interpretation of core-periphery relations in Marxist literary critic Benita Parry’s reading of world systems theory by Immanuel Wallerstein, Samir Amin and others; Parry uses this reading to understand the aesthetic affinity in peripheral countries due to a similar past experience in colonialism and capitalism, which according to her gives birth to stylistic irregularities in art. Many stylistic irregularities in these novels are examples of both how the meaning and value of core and periphery change over time, whether it be in a nation, or in global geographical dispensation; and how literary and artistic works register these changes and play the complexities of historical modernity into their narrative fabric.Keywords: core-periphery, stylistic irregularities, novel form, post-independence India.

openalex_display_name: Representation of Implicit Domestic Culture in Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi
openalex_abstract: Exploring implicit domestic culture in Twilight in Delhi (2007)by Ahmed Ali, the study applies theoretical framework of M.A.K Halliday’s Systemic Functional Grammar (SFG) which asserts that meanings lies in the clause. The main argument of the paper is to linguistically examine the effects of social imbalance within family structure. It also argues that language is not neutral for it carries ideology in it; therefore, hegemonic power relations and its manipulation are explored leading to its effects on different lives.Data are analyzed qualitatively at clause level, using tools of ideational, interpersonal and textual meta-functions of language.As a guide, 19 Tables are formed to show and compares the processes according to the main issue of the study. Linguistic analysis of the text is done by using Transitivity, Mood, Rheme and Theme to identify power relations in Eastern families. The paper examined different sorts of 19 situations where the norms of implicit family culture were noticed. The study also discovered that the male members of the family exercised power over the female characters. The study is going to be an addition to future researchers of CDA to use SFG to literature to highlight and analyze social imbalance.

openalex_display_name: Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi: A Polyphonic Novel
openalex_abstract: This paper explores diverse voices inAli’s “Twilight in Delhi”(1940) throughBakhtin’s theory of dialogism (1994). Multiple voices coexist in the novel in different situations. This paper aims at investigatingthe situations where the voices are amalgamated. This paper also examines the effect of this fusion of voices on the socio-political atmosphere of Delhi. Close reading technique helped in retrieval of eighteen situations in the novelwhere voices are fused, and then the actions and reactions of the characters in the novel were qualitatively probed. The paper findsthatmultiple voices in the novel exist and enhances the effect of the authorial voice. The study will contribute to get an insight into the situation in India, and how the two groups impersonated as the English and the Indian showed verbally their reactions. It will also help future researchers to view the narrative from dialogic point of view.

openalex_display_name: Gender and Domestic Space in Ahmed Ali's and Krishna Sobti's Novels on Old Delhi
openalex_abstract: Female perspective and agency in Delhi from the 1920s to the 1940s do not usually find mention with regard to novels written about that significant period. Much celebrated novels such as Twilight in Delhi by Ahmed Ali and The Heart Has Its Reasons by Krishna Sobti are usually viewed as nostalgic evocations of the lost past of the city as it was moving out of colonial rule and into a new era. This paper examines the complexities of gender relations and segregation as offered in the novels, which mirror and showcase the gradual intensification of the colonised city shifting into a space of independence, although at first with timid hesitation. It displays the novels as structuring and perpetuating gendered relationships between women and men as also, importantly, between women in the household and those outside it. While published in markedly different times, the everyday lived realities of the time as explored in Delhi’s literary landscape by Ali and Sobti exhibit great similarities in the gendered ramifications of female dispossession as per policy, and the economic implications of women’s property being in the hands of “their” men. Transformations in the city space influence domestic spaces, impacting the female characters. In examining these socio-spatial segregations in early urban Delhi literature, the paper opens the field for further research on economic systems in literary texts.

openalex_display_name: Literature as a Form of Resistance Against British Colonial Rule in India
openalex_abstract: This thesis concentrates on literature during India's battle for independence from the British Empire. These publications look at the outcomes of Europe's intent to colonize and its impact on the marginalized, colonial subjects down to the personal level. Delving into the tragic reality of colonialism and investigating its impact as portrayed in the novels selected, this thesis argues that the selected texts operate as resistance literature subverting the colonial discourse in retrieving South Asian culture and history. This project explores specific forms of resistance within the tropes of memory, history, and gender to pose a larger question of decolonial futures in the postcolonial aftermath. The explorations of Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi, Rabindranath Tagore's The Home and the World, and R.K. Narayan's Waiting for the Mahatma all represent multiple ways of studying the independence movement in their resistance frame. Analyzing these works through a postcolonial perspective unveils underrepresented voices and the intricacies of the Independence landscape. Ahmed Ali incorporates nostalgia as an argument for abolition and articulates Muslim identity in India's rapidly transforming environment. Tagore writes from his real experiences, recounting the confusion and disarray that plagued the Independence movement as disputes erupted on how to fight for India's sovereignty. R.K. Narayan embraces the ‘Quit India' protest and Gandhi's pacifist ideals while worrying about the future after the Mahatma's death. These writers decolonize readers' minds, and campaign for India's independence against the Empire Such literature gives the colonized a voice as they actively resist the British colonization in every aspect of existence.

openalex_display_name: Humayun Kabir, Men and Rivers, and Faridpur
openalex_abstract: In the history of South Asian literature in English, Men and Rivers is the third fictional work written by a Muslim author after Rokeya's Sultana's Dream and Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi (1940). Men and Rivers is a literary work of great merit though more research needs to be conducted on the work to appreciate its value by examining various thematic and stylistic features. Through Men and Rivers, Hamayun Kabir conferred on Faridpur literary immortality. I believe the novel will continue to make the district memorable and special to its readers for a very long time.

openalex_display_name: Bilingualism in Pakistani Fiction: The Analysis of Twilight in Delhi by Ahmed Ali
openalex_abstract: This research aims to find code-switching occurrences in Twilight in Delhi written by Pakistani English postcolonial writer Ahmed Ali. He uses many Urdu terms and expressions in his narrative to keep alive Eastern culture and traditions that would otherwise lose their essence if translated into English. In this way, he reconstitutes English language in his work. The frequency of Urdu words is recorded, and the data obtained is analyzed on semantic, phonological and syntactic grounds. The writer also tries to experiment with the form and brings creativity, and in doing so, he applies English structure on Urdu terms and introduced a new vocabulary. The deliberate use of code-switching in the novel shows that language is no one’s property neither someone’s hegemony.

openalex_display_name: Stylistic Deviations in Ali's Twilight in Delhi (2007)
openalex_abstract: This study investigates stylistic deviations in Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi (2007), highlighting how the author employs non-standard English features to create a distinct narrative style. Drawing on stylistics theory (Leech & Short, 1981) and research on Pakistani English (Rahman, 1990; Baumgardner, 1993), the paper analyzes deviations in syntax, lexis, and semantics, including tense variations, prepositional and article usage, hybridization, preposed phrases, and semantic shifts. The study adopts a qualitative, descriptive approach, identifying and categorizing deviations to examine their narrative and cultural functions. Findings suggest that these deviations not only reflect local linguistic identity but also enhance the novel’s stylistic richness and reader engagement.

openalex_display_name: Reclaiming the City’s Nature: An Ecocritical Reading of Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi.
openalex_abstract: Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi (1940) provides a rare opportunity to explore how literature can register ecological concerns in the midst of colonial upheaval. While the novel is conventionally examined for its historical and political insights, it also offers a subtle meditation on the interdependence between human societies and their environments. This paper undertakes an ecocritical reading of Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi (1940), exploring the complex intersections between urban space, nature, and colonial modernity. While the novel is often studied for its historical, political, and cultural resonances, its ecological dimensions remain largely overlooked. By situating the narrative within the framework of ecocriticism, this study examines how Ali juxtaposes the natural environment with the decaying cityscape of colonial Delhi. The imagery of gardens, flowers, seasons, and the Yamuna River not only evokes nostalgia for a precolonial past but also reveals the ways in which colonial urbanization disrupts the organic relationship between humans and nature. Nature in the novel functions as both a site of cultural memory and a metaphor for dispossession, reflecting the erosion of traditional lifeways under imperial domination. At the same time, the persistent presence of natural cycles resists colonial temporality, offering subtle forms of resilience and renewal. Ultimately, this reading argues that Twilight in Delhi reclaims the city’s nature as an integral part of its cultural and historical identity, challenging the erasures of colonial modernity and foregrounding ecological consciousness in the discourse of decolonization. His vision highlights how rivers, gardens, and ecological cycles function as living archives of memory and resistance, while also warning of their vulnerability to neglect and exploitation. In connecting ecocriticism with postcolonial critique, the novel speaks to ongoing debates about ecological justice, sustainability, and the reclamation of urban ecologies in the Global South. It demonstrates that decolonization must be conceived not only as political freedom but also as the recovery of ecological balance and integrity.

openalex_display_name: TWILIGHT IN DELHI AND INDIAN NATIONALISM
openalex_abstract: India is a large country. British India was bigger in size and population. Our history is bright. Chandragupta Maurya of Patna conquered the large territory amicably. After the decline of the Maurya dynasty, the vast kingdom could not remain united. Alauddin Khilji re-organised the fragmented pieces, thus formulating one vast India again. Such a position continued from the Sultanat period to the Mughal period. The descendants of Aurangzeb could not protect the nation and themselves. Britishers were like traders up to 1757, however they observed their scope in Indian polity. They were guided by their Headquarter London, whereas Indian rulers were dis-united. The Indian renaissance started during the early nineteenth century. English writing by any Indian was started by Dean Mohammad of Patna during 1794. His book The Travels of Dean Mahomet is perhaps the first English book by any Indian. Social reform through Indian English fiction was started during the early twentieth century. Sultana's Dream (1905) by Rokaya Sakhawat Husain is a land-mark. The English novel Rajmohan's wife by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay was superseded by his Bengali novels. Indian English novel writing, in true sense, starts during the fourth decade of the twentieth century. Mulk Raj Anand, R.K. Narayan, Raja Rao and Ahmed Ali contributed a lot in this literary genre. Ahmed Ali's first novel Twilight in Delhi was published during 1940, followed by his second novel Ocean of Night (1964) and the last novel Of Rats and Diplomats (1985). These all novels are sincere look towards the present and the future of the nation.

openalex_display_name: Resemblance of Societies in Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi and Achebe’s Things Fall Apart
openalex_abstract: The main aim of the paper is to create awareness about socio- political cultures of societies. It portrays the degradation of culture, vanishing of some practices. Secondary data for this study were collected from a variety of sources, including books, journals, articles and other sources. Characters in both the novels portray culture. The researchers used Analytical Method and Descriptive Method. Colonization created numerous opportunities for the colonizers to sow division among the colonized for their own economic -political gain. The colonial discourse produced by western writers mainly centered on the culture, life style and traditions of colonized people , often depicting them as inferior. In contrast, Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart in particular questions colonial representations. This paper therefore examines Achebe's representation of Igbo culture, and Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi's traditional societies. Literature, along with other cultural expressions, serves as a main tool to portray historical events. It explores socio-cultural transformation which took place in 20th century India. It depicts the decaying traditional culture of old Delhi while illustrating how emerging India's sociocultural and political fabric. Ahmed Ali focuses on themes like time, memory, identity, culture, colonization and social change.

openalex_display_name: Tracing the Socio-Political Trends of Socialist Thought in Pre-Partition South Asian English Fiction: Historical Contexts and Literary Narratives
openalex_abstract: The paper discusses the socio-political tendencies of socialism in the pre-partition South Asian English fiction of Mulk Raj Anand in the texts of Untouchable (1935), Coolie (1936) and Two Leaves and a Bud (1937), Ahmed Ali in the text Twilight in Delhi (1940) and Raja Rao in the novel Kanthapara (1938). The study traces the theme of these novels in relation to the socio-political paradigm of colonial South Asia based on the historical circumstances, the theme of the novels and the manner in which they highlight the issue of class relations, labour exploitation, structural inequality, social decline and collective action. It has been evident throughout the discussion that Anand is a realist in his narratives, Ali illustrates how structural change is affecting the old hierarchies and that Rao is a Gandhian in her storytelling with a different model of the political mobilization. The combination of these pieces of writing demonstrates that early South Asian English fiction did not shy away of the socio-political arguments of the pre-partition era but reflected in a variety of albeit simultaneously related views on justice, inequality and social change. This research paper is a contribution to the current body of scholarship because it predicts the importance of class and labour as the primary categories of early English fiction reading in the region.

openalex_display_name: Negotiating Colonial Modernity: Material Culture, Cultural Memory, and Everyday Identity Formation in Ahmed Ali’s Twilight in Delhi
openalex_abstract: Colonialism in South Asia operated not only through political domination and economic exploitation but also through cultural transformations that reshaped identities, social relations, and everyday practices. This article examines Ahmed Ali's Twilight in Delhi (1940) as a cultural text that captures the complex negotiations between colonial power, indigenous traditions, and emerging forms of modernity in late-colonial India. Drawing on New Historicism and postcolonial cultural theory, the article argues that Ali's novel represents colonialism as a process that penetrated ordinary cultural practices, material objects, linguistic hierarchies, and domestic spaces. Rather than presenting colonial rule merely as an external political force, the novel reveals how colonial modernity reshaped everyday cultural practices, producing new negotiations of identity, memory, and belonging. Through close textual analysis, the study explores how British colonial authority transformed Delhi's social imagination, disrupted Mughal cultural memory, and generated tensions between inherited traditions and colonial modernity. By bringing New Historicist analysis into dialogue with postcolonial perspectives on power, representation, and cultural identity, this study extends existing scholarship on Twilight in Delhi beyond narratives of decline and nostalgia, focusing instead on everyday cultural practices and material objects. It demonstrates how colonial modernity produced simultaneous processes of displacement, adaptation, and cultural negotiation. It argues that Twilight in Delhi should be read as a cultural archive of colonial modernity in Asia, where everyday practices, material objects, and urban spaces reveal the uneven negotiations between imperial power and indigenous forms of knowledge. By examining these everyday negotiations, the article contributes to broader debates in Asian cultural studies on colonial afterlives, cultural memory, and the production of modern identities.

openalex_display_name: Irish Children's Literature and the Poetics of Memory by Rebecca Long
openalex_abstract: Reviewed by: Irish Children's Literature and the Poetics of Memory by Rebecca Long Julie Anne Stevens (bio) Irish Children's Literature and the Poetics of Memory. By Rebecca Long. Bloomsbury Academic, 2021. Rebecca Long frames her study of memory and mythmaking in twentieth- and twenty-first century Irish children's literature within a nationalist discourse: Ireland's late-nineteenth-century [End Page 116] enterprise to create an identity through collecting and retelling Irish myths. In four chapters, she describes the retrieving, retelling, remembering, and reimagining of Irish myths and folklore from the 1890s Revival period up until 2016 with Ireland's centenary of the Easter Rising. This frame suggests the extent to which Irish children's literature has been directed by the cultural nationalism of the Celtic Revival. However, Long's interest lies not so much in the political or social significance of the Irish myths in children's literature as in the act and the significance of remembering. Memory and memory studies are her focus. Moreover, although she emphasizes the Revival when Douglas Hyde, Lady Gregory, W. B. Yeats, and many others re-visioned Irish folklore and myth in their writings, her scholarship lies more with contemporary material. I say this because her first chapter on the Revivalists seems to me to have been shaped to suit later concerns in her study. She appears to be looking backwards at this time, choosing material which best reveals more recent interests in Irish children's literature and myth. She selects, for instance, the retelling of Cuchulainn's exploits by Standish O'Grady and Lady Gregory in the 1890s even though these versions were not aimed at children but written for a general audience. (She could have looked at O'Grady's 1892 children's book Finn and His Companions instead, for example.) However, later important Irish children's books revisit Cuchulainn's adventures, thus emphasizing the repetition of certain stories, which Long sees as central in the processes of cultural memory. Despite the selective nature of Long's assessment of the 1890s Revivalists, she provides a compelling argument regarding Irish children's literature's central preoccupation with remembering myth and folklore. Following upon critical studies such as Young Irelands (2011) edited by Mary Shine Thompson, or more general studies such as Folklore and Modern Irish Writing (2014) edited by Anne Markey and Anne O'Connor, Long argues the importance of the Irish myths in relation to Irish childhood and Irish identity. In so doing, Long explores the importance of orality and, perhaps even more compelling, the central significance of landscape in relation to memory in Irish children's literature about myth. Long's second chapter on retelling folklore in children's books shows how much the early nation state emphasized its "lost mythological heritage" (45). openalex_abstract: T he Saturday Evening Post rose rapidly to become a prominent national magazine in the first decades of the twentieth century. Its editor, George Horace Lorimer, shepherded the magazine’s growth with a firm hand and a finger on the pulse of America. One key indicator of Lorimer’s extraordinary ability to connect with his readers was “Letters from a Self-Made Merchant” and its successor “Old Gorgon Graham,” which ran from 1901 to 1904. These were written anonymously by Lorimer himself and were so popular that they were later published as a book. They took the form of letters written by John “Old Gorgon” Graham to his son. As the title suggests Graham had worked his way up from scratch to own a grand meat-packing firm. With the changes sweeping a swiftly industrializing America, Lorimer could have used this platform to address many pressing social issues, such as the labor problem or the trust question. Significantly, though, the letters centered on another problem that Lorimer must have considered of grave import to his readers—the passing of the torch from the self-made men to a new generation of leaders (often more-privileged sons).
